speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Is that mostly in bars?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would, I think, be mostly in bars, because under modern conditions gold is handled more in bars than in coin, but the point I desire to make is that over this period of three years the officials of the Finance Department have handled- that enormous amount of gold involving all that detailed work with no expense whatever to the Bank of England or the Imperial Government, with the exception of a few hundred dollars for cartage. I am not making this statement in order that any credit may devolve upon myself or the Government, but I do feel that I should make the statement in simple justice to the men of that department who have devoted themselves unsparingly day and night to the duties of their office.
In addition to handling that gold for account of the Bank of England the department has been indirectly concerned-and here I desire to pay a tribute to the officials of the mint rather than to those of my department-with the operations carried on by the mint at Ottawa. It will surprise the House, I have no doubt, to learn that we have in Ottawa Mint a refinery for the refining of raw gold which has the largest capacity of any refinery in the world. That is due to the fact that about a year and a half ago the mint was enlarged in order that we might treat gold from South Africa
and Russia which had not been refined to a sufficient degree of fineness when it reached this country. Late in May, 1916, plans and preparations were made for an extension of the refinery, and in seven weeks the extension was completed and in operation. The present capacity is 250,000 ounces or $5,000,000 per week, and the method employed is what is known as the chlorine process. Since September, 1915, there has been received at the, mint- $225,000,000 in raw gold, practically all of which has been refined and delivered, which work has been done in addition to the regular work required at the mint.
The work of the officials of my department who have been immediately concerned has not ended there w'ith receiving this gold. Under instructions from the Imperial Government, that gold has been moved, to the amoupt of hundreds otf millions, to New YotIj. Great care was required in weighing oiut, >in shipment, and in the attention necessary in connection with the sending of this gold forward by express. As I have stated, over $1,000,000,000 of treasure has been handled and distributed, a staggering sum,, I suppose probably twice the amount of gold in the United Kingdom at the outbreak of the war.
In addition to the service in connection with these transactions, an immense volume of detailed work and responsibility has devolved upon the officials of my department in connection with the domestic loans. Before the war broke out all our financing was done in Londlon. The loans were arranged by our financial agents there, the Banlk of Montreal, after cable communication with the minister or deputy minister. The detailed work connected with these loans was carried out, of course, by the staff of the Bank of Montreal in London. The House is aware that since the outbreak of the war we have placed three domestic kwanfe in Canada. The first loan was for $50,000,000 increased to $100,000,000. The securities issued were in denominations of $100, $500, and $1,000. The next loan w>as for $100,000,000, and in connection with that loan applications to the >amount of over $200,000,000 were received, with deposit payments in connection therewith., of course. In M'airoh of this year we issued another loan of $150,000,000 and in connection with that offer applications to the amount of $250,000,000 were received. Besides the deposit payments, of course, these several loans were subsequently all paid up. All this Is well known to the House,



bu't that wlhioh is not known, and could not be known except through a statement made by	the	minister ot
some one else on behalf of the department, is the enormous amount of work devolving upon the officials of the department in connection with these loans. Subscriptions might be sent in through any branch of any of the chartered banks of Canada, aui there are about 3,500 of these branches. Not only did the department keep account with practically all of these branch banks, because subscriptions were received through nearly all, but it was actually necessary to keep an account, so to say, with each bond itself, in order that the transaction might be correctly handled. The banks, as agents of the Finance Department, issued provisional receipts. These receipts had to be prepared and sent to the banks by the department. Then scrip had to be issued as a provisional security. This was prepared in the department and forwarded to the banks ready for those who had subscribed to the loan. Then, as the instalments on the payments were made, the department was notified, and, of course, the necessary accounts had to be kept in the department. Ultimately, the bonds had to be engraved and forwarded to the several banks in exchange for the outstanding certificates. Take for example, the last loan. There were forty thousand subscribers, and over two hundred thousand separate pieces of scrip were delivered in connection with that transaction. Of course, a great deal of the routine work is done by temporary help; we have had to greatly increase our staff to meet the situation. >But the heavy and responsible work in connection with these loans has been done by a handful of men in the department; the deputy minister, the assistant deputy minister, the comptroller of the currency, and the chief officials in the office. These men have given themselves to the duties of their position in a manner that has commanded my admiration, and I feel that I should be lacking in simple justice to the staff and to the Civil Service if I did not bear this testimony and have it placed upon record. To my knowledge some of these men have permanently injured their health,-I am not in tire least exaggerating the situation. The public do not know and cannot know the strain imposed upon certain departments of the Government in time of war. I should like it to be known when this war is over that the officials of the Department of Fi-

nance have acquitted themselves in 'the manner I have indicated.
Let me say something of the staff itself. All this work has been accomplished with comparatively little increase in the number of the staff of the department; so far as the leading officials are concerned, there are actually fewer than there were at the outbreak of the war. The organization of the Finance Department when the war began included the deputy minister, the assistant deputy, o( whom I sbaM say a few words in a moment, tfhe accountant, Mr. Sauniders, and the comptroller of dominion currency, Mr. Rourke. Of these principal officials all are there to-day with the exception of Mr. Ross, who has been lost to the department. He was a great official, 'being a man of high character and fine ability. When I was in England in November last I received a cable from Mr. Ross stating that he had received a very attractive offer. He was not willing to leave the service, but I think that he felt that in justice to his family he should submit the situation to me. Though I knew I should miss him very greatly, and though I knew that the loss to the service would be great, I felt that I should not stand in his way, and I so cabled him. The result is that Mr. Ross is now the secretary of the Canadian Bankers' Association, enjoying a much larger salary than he would have obtained in the service of the Dominion. The executive work of the Finance Department is oauried on by the deputy minister, the assistant deputy, Mr. Saunders, and the comptroller of the currency, Mr. Rourke, and certain other leading officials to whom I haVe referred.
As to the particular item under discussion, I may ,say that Mr. Ross received as assistant deputy minister a salary of $4,500 a year. I filled the position by promotion. I did not go outside of the department. If I had gone outside of the department into the financial world to fill the position occupied by Mr. Ross, I have no hesitation in saying that I should have been obliged to pay $7,000 or $8,000 in order to obtain a man who could fill that position. I know something of the salaries obtained in the financial World and obtained for financial skill. I would have been obliged to pay much more than $4,500 in order to get a man to fill that position, and I am not sure that I could have got a man to properly fill that position, because the knowledge of financial administration in connection with the Government is not found except at Ottawa. So that Mr. Ross's position was filled by the promotion

of Mr. Saunders, who had been for many years Dominion accountant, and who was thoroughly versed in the financial affairs of the Dominion. I submit that was an eminently proper course for me to pursue. A very deserving man was appointed to the position, and I gave him the same salary that Mr. Ross obtained, because there is one less official in the Department of Finance. Then, Mr. Rourke, who has had most to do with the movement of gold and who is an excellent official, assiduous in his devotion to his duties and highly skilled, was advanced also to the same salary of $4,500. In the re-arrangement of the staff I doubt if there is any increase in the total of the salaries of the executive officers as a whole.
If I have any fault to find with the Finance Department, it is that there are not enough principal officers. When I was in charge of a business I always used to insist upon an understudy for every important position, and I believe in plenty of help and well paid help. You will never have a highly efficient Finance Department, or any other highly efficient department of the Government, until you are willing to pay men reasonable salaries for skilled service. As far as this particular item relating to the salary of the assistant deputy minister is concerned, it is precisely the same as it was before. The controller of the Dominion currency has been advanced to $4,500, and my opinion is that he is underpaid to-day -substantially underpaid-for the service which he renders. Then we have another item, that of "Accountant Contingencies," at $3,000. The accountant of contingencies is Mr. Brittain. Mr. Brittain until last year was in the second division grade "A", and had gone up to the maximum of the division, namely, $2,800. The House may know that among the other duties which have developed upon me since the outbreak of the war are those connected with the position of honorary treasurer of the Patriotic Fund. Some $23,000,000 or $24,000,000 have been subscribed to the fund by the patriotic people of Canada, and there is a very great deal of work connected with the administration of the fund in my office. All the moneys are paid into the honorary treasurer and they are checked out by the Finance Department to the several organizations throughout the country for the purposes of the fund. The .official who has had to do with that work is Mr. Brittain and Mr. Brittain has literally laboured day and night, in season and out, in connection with that work. The Cana-
114 J
dian Patriotic Fund, about a year and a half agp, offered to give Mr. Brittain a gratuity of $1,000 in recognition of his patriotic service in connection with the fund. Mr. Brittain declined to accept that gratuity. He said that he preferred that his work should go to the fund, that that was his contribution. When I had under consideration the question of salaries this year, I thought it only fair to Mr. Brittain, who is an excellent official and quite entitled upon his merits as an officer apart from the duties devolving upon him in connection with the Patriotic Fund, that he should go into the first division of class " A " and should receive a salary of $3,000. I doubt if any hon. member of this House will raise any objection to Mr. Brittain being recognized by advancement to a position having a salary of $3,000. In addition, we have the commissioner of taxation at $5,000 and the assistant commissioner of taxation at $3,500. In connection with my department in ordinary times there is what is known as the Tariff Branch. It requires experienced and skilled men to be competent tariff officers and I believe I am fortunate in having two of the ablest tariff men in this country in my department. Both men had long experience in connection with the Customs before entering the Department of Finance. One is Mr. Russell and the other is Mr. Breadner. With Mr. Breadner, with Mr. Russell and with John McDougald, who is a great official, one of the greatest officials this country has ever produced, and who holds the office of Commissioner of Customs, this country is exceptionally well equipped in tariff officers. I doubt if *any country is better equipped or served by tariff experts than Canada is by the Commissioner of Customs and the two gentlemen I have named. It is the duty of these men in the Tariff Branch to keep in touch with tariff matters, with general business and industry, with prices and with the tariffs of otheT countries so that we have at all times information in respect to matters that may be .of importaance in connection with the tariff. Last year I introduced the Business Pirofits War Tax Act and its administration has devolved very responsible duties upon my department. In the organization which was created to carry out the legislation we appointed Mr. Breadner as commissioner of taxation and Mr. Russell as assistant commissioner of taxation. These men have had in addition to their ordinary duties the responsibility of administering the Business Profits

War Tax Act, a very responsible duty indeed. They have had to organize, practically over the entire, c.ountry, a staff for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act and of levying and collecting the tax. I bear tribute to the faithfulness and ability with which they have carried out their duties. But the point I desire to make now is that there has been added to them since last year the administration of this Act. In recognition of that fact, and of the additional duties and responsibilities devolving upon them, their salaries have been increased by $500 in both cases, Mr. Breadner from $4,500 to $5,000 and Mr. Bussell from $3,000 to $3,500. These are the [DOT]circumstances with the increases which are indicated in this item in the Estimates now before the committee. I submit that the work of the department has greatly increased, that the staff have fully risen to the occasion, and that all the members of the staff whose names are mentioned here and with whose cases I have dealt in this brief statement before the committee are deserving of the appointments which they have received and of the salaries attached to the positions.

Without in any way
diverging from the question, may I ask at this point if in the collection of the war tax there are many cases pending where people have refused to pay and action has been taken by the department, or if the administration has been smooth, and every one has paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The administration of the Business Profits War Tax has been most satisfactory. The public who have been subjected to the taxation have been more than, willing to pay their contributions-they have been anxious to pay. There have been practically no cases of dispute between the department and those assessed. That arises from the fact that in most cases the capital is comparatively easily established; the profits are made known from the accounting statement, and the rest is a 'matter of mathematical calculation. But there are, of course, many cases in which a difference of opinion would arise and in which difference of opinion has arisen with regard to capitalization; and there have been some cases of dispute as to the amount which might reasonably be allowed for depreciation under the Act. A number of cases of that kind are always pending. But when the matter has been .brought to my attention and we have gone into the facts fully and have had the parties to

Ottawa and fully considered the situation, there have been almost no cases in which we did not reach a conclusion that was satisfactory to the department. There has been no disposition on the part of the public to resist the taxation'in any way; in fact, the contrary has been the case; they have been anxious and desirous to pay, and I hope that it will not be necessary to litigate any cases in connection with that taxation. On the whole, I think the impression has been that the department has administered the tax very fairly and reasonably, always with a due regard to the provisions of the Act, which, of course, it is our duty to enforce strictly.
I do not know that it is 'necessary for me to say anything further. I am glad in a way that my hon. friend raised the question of the salaries, because it has given me an opportunity of making a statement which I feel that I should make in reference to the staff. I do not believe that any of these salaries are high, having regard to the skill required, the responsible nature of the duties devolving upon the officials. On the contrary, I believe they are considerably below the salares paid in financial institutions outside. I am positive as to that, and I make the statement again which I made this afternoon, that I do not believe there is any financial institution in this country which could have handled the gold shipments, of which I have made special mention, and the domestic loans, aggregating $350,000,000, as efficiently as the officials of the Finance Department have handled that business. Just in connection with the loans, let me point out that there were not only the $350,000,000 of war loan issues, but in addition to that, over 100,000 of the small war saving certificates have been issued. I am sure the House will be pleased to learn that within the last three months the public of this country have subscribed for over 100,000 of these $25, $50, and $100 war savings certificates, aggregating over $7,000,000 in gross amount. Those represent for the most part subscriptions by those of comparatively slender means. They were anxious to contribute of their resources to the Government in order to aid in the prosecution of the war. In addition to that, they will have their savings in that form of investment, and that may be a matter of considerable importance to the country, especially having regard to the conditions that may prevail after the war is over.

The Minister of Finance entirely misconceived the criticism which I

made against his action in over-riding, as I said, the provisions of the Civil Service Act, and including these amounts in the estimates in the way he has done. The only answer he has made is that the department has had a great deal of important work to attend to. I do not dispute that. But other departments have also had very important work to do. Take the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I understand that its work has been very great, and necessarily it would be greatly increased by reason of the war. But I do not understand that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries is recommending that in the case of his officials the Civil Service Act should be disregarded.
I do not understand that his officials are asking for that. I understand that they, having taken their offices under the Civil Service Act, have been quite content to perform their duties and to take the increases which the Act proviides. So I thought that the Department of Militia had been very greatly worked and overworked during the war. I do not imagine that there is any official of the Government who has had a greater strain put upon him by the war than General Fiset, the Deputy Minister of Militia. But his minister is not recommending that the Civil Service Act should be overridden in his case. He is not asking for special consideration, or a special vote of Parliament. Apparently the Minister of Militia recognizes that in these times of stress, when everybody has to suffer, when many people have to do a great deal of work for very little'pay, and everybody has to live on very much less than he required before the war, the officials of that department are willing to perform their duties without asking that the law should be violated. When the Minister of Finance, with his broad and generous views upon financial questions, accustomed to big salaries, many times be-yound what this Government has been paying to its officials, comes in and asks that, with respect to his department, an exception shall be made, that the law shall be overridden, the reasons for the establishment of thb Civil Service Act by Parliament shall be ignored, and that these gentlemen who have been in the service a very short time shall receive for limited service the same salaries as other officials who have been giving splendid work to the country for a great many years. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance speaks of the work that has been done; and I am willing to recognize the importance of it, and the splendid way in which it has been done; I am willing to join in testimony to
the officials of the Finance Department for their energy, capability, and devotion to duty. But I desire, also, to say to the Dominion Government and the people of Canada that they ought to be proud of the Civil Service at Ottawa in all departments, and I have had occasion to know the way in which they perform their duties. I say that in all the departments the Government and people of this country are getting splendid service at, in most instances, a very low remuneration for the duties which are performed by the Civil Service.
But the Minister of Finance has forgotten to tell the committee that he has in his department now .117 employees, as against 104 last year.
While there is much responsibility in the 1 andling of gold bars, i take it that the assistant deputy minister, the comptroller of dominion currency and the accountant of contingencies are not very much occupied in handling them. Very large responsibility rests upon the efficient Deputy Minister of Finance in connection with these matters, but he is getting no increase. Is there any official in the department, who has the same degree of responsibility as the deputy minister? Under the Civil Service Act he is entitled to $5,000 a year; apparently he is contented with that. New men are brought into the department and given substantially the same-in one instance exactly the same-as the deputy minister receives, who has been in the department for a great many years. The deputy minister has grown old in the service; to my knowledge he has done splendid work. My hon. friend referred to the great work of the mint. His department has nothing to do with the mint, which is a department of the Imperial Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I paid a tribute to the work of the mint.

My hon. friend did so with the view of throwing a halo round himself and his department. The mint was established by the late Government, in the face of a great deal of criticism on the part of hon. gentlemen then of the Opposition. The mint is doing splendid work, hut it is a department of the Imperial Government; therefore its work does not in any way add to the work which the officials of the Finance Department are performing. My criticism is that equally good and equally important work is being done in other departments; that it is contrary to the principles upon which the Civil Service Act

was based and contrary to the spirit which ought to animate the Government in the administration of that Act that certain officials should receive exceptional treatment as against other equally hard-worked officials. The salaries proposed to be given to the assistant deputy minister and the comptroller of dominion currency, $4,500, and the commissioner of taxation, $5,000, are not warranted by the Civil Service Act. My hon.. friend knows that he is acting contrary to the provisions of the Civil Service Act when he comes to Parliament and asks for this vote. He has referred to Mr. John McDougald, Commissioner of Customs, as a splendid official. So he is, but he has given his whole life to the service of the country, and, splendid official as he is, the Minister of Finance has not asked for an increase for him. Not one dollar is to be added to his salary, notwithstanding the length of his service and the great work that he has done. Yet this young man who was appointed commissioner of taxation, coming into the department only in recent years, receives the same salary as Mr. McDougald, whom my hon. friend has eulogized.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend not know that 'Mr. Breadner has been thirty years in the Dominion service?
Well, I suppose Mr. McDougald has been fifty years in the service.

speechtext:
Oh, no, he was in this
House not so very many years ago.
Pretty nearly fifty years, then.

speechtext: Twenty years.

Mr. Breadner was in a subordinate position in the Customs Department, while Mr. McDougald occupies a position next to the minister. Besides, Mr. Breadner was out of the service for a while, being employed by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: He was twenty-six years in the service before he went with the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. He has been back about four years.

speechtext: About four years, but he has been in the service about thirty years altogether.

I should not like to say anything that would even appear to be a [Mr. Pugsley. I
criticism of Mr. Breadner, for I recognize that he is an excellent official. But the Minister of Finance is taking Mr. Breadner outside of the Civil Service Act, and he is leaving Mr. McDougald under its provisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman does not know that Mr. Breadner was getting a salary of $4,500 a year from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association at the time he returned to the service.

I suppose he was, but he chose to come back to the service of the Government. There must be attractions in the Government service. Mr. Butler, who was Deputy Minister of Railways and Canals for quite a long time, could have obtained outside the Government service at any time twice the salary that he was receiving in the department. In the Department of Public Works, for instance, the chief engineer, the assistant to the chief engineer, or the superintendent of dredging would, I am told, receive from private companies or firms very much larger salaries than they receive in the service of the Government. But they are not treated with any special favour; they are compelled to accept the increases which the Civil Service Act provides. The comptroller of currency, to whom the minister referred, has not been a long time in the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Twenty-two years.

The Chief Accountant in the Department of Public Works, who handles millions of dollars every year, and whose duties are very heavy indeed, receives only $3,625. Since the Civil Service Act came into force he has been obliged to accept the increases provided by that Act. I mention him because I happen to know the very important duties which he has performed. He is not complaining-I am not speaking at his instance, for I have not been communicated with by anybody-but I am endeavouring to point out to the minister that great dissatisfaction is liable to be caused in the Civil Service by this discrimination-by applying the Civil Service Act to some officials and not to others. Hundreds of employees in the Civil Service, who are working at from $900 to $1,200 per year, are deserving of increases. They are hardly able to keep soul and body together in these days of the high cost of living, yet they cannot get any increase; they must remain under the terms of the Civil Service Act, getting increases through length of ser-

vice only as the Act provides. I do not complain that the gentlemen to whom I have referred are getting more than they are entitled to or more than they would get if engaged with firms or companies carrying on business. What I object to is the discrimination which the minister is exercising towards these gentlemen as against others in the service who are equally deserving and who discharge equally as important duties. The minister sought to show that the issuing of scrip takes up an enormous amount of time. One would almost think that these gentlemen had to write the scrip in their own handwriting or on a typewriter. My hon. friend knows that this scrip is all printed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know anything of the kind.
Or lithographed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend does not know what he is talking about when he says that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Scrip is partly printed, but the names, payments, etc., have to he filled in, and this involves an immense amount of work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That is enough, too.

Then it is all printed or lithographed, with the exception of certain blanks, which have to be filled in. This work could be done by any clerk receiving a salary of $500 a year. It is not work that requires any broad intellect.
I venture to say that my friend the deputy minister or those gentlemen who are receiving increases in salary would devote very little attention to that work, and that it would be done by some one of those hundred odd employees who are in the service of the department and who are receiving the smaller salaries. Let us take the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and let us take Mr. Anderson, the chief engineer as an instance. Mr. Anderson has been in the service for a great many years; he is discharging duties of a very important character: he is supervising the expenditure of millions of dollars of the people's money; he occupies a position where keen judgment, strict integrity and great devotion are required; yet all he receives under the Civil Service Act is $4,000 a year, and he cannot
get one dollar beyond that amount because that is the highest salary attaching to the head of a department next to the deputy minister. Yet, notwithstanding the fact that my hon. friend has a full knowledge of the long service that Mr. Anderson and men like him have given to the country, my hon. friend here gives to this comparatively young man a boost of $1,000 over and above what he receives under the Civil Service Act. In the Department of Public Works, Mr. Ewart, the chief architect, who has been for forty years, perhaps longer, in the department and who is a most faithful oflicial, cannot receive more than $4,000 a year. In the Department of Kailways, the chief engineer, I think, although I am not quite sure, receives only $4,000 a year. Mr. Dufresne, who was brought to the Department of Public Works from Winnipeg receives only $4,000 a year, although he is doing work of a very important character, and the supervising engineer, Mr. Valiquet, receives only $3,600 a year. All these gentlemen are doing very important work, and work which I think might be just as well recognized as the work which is being performed by those gentlemen in the Department of Finance; but the Minister of Finance is generous; he is apparently looking after his employees all the time; he does-not care what the Civil Service Act provides for; he apparently does not care how the employees of the other departments of Government are treated; he has broad and generous views in regard to his own department, and he asks this committee to favour certain officials in his department, and to leave the others to plod along as best they can, bound by the Civil Service Act. It is for that reason, I find fault with the (minister and not because for the work those gentlemen are performing they are highly paid; it is because I think there ought to be certain general rules which should apply to all the departments, and the Civil Service Act having been brought into operation to prevent discrim-9 p.m. ination taking place, to prevent favouritism, and to have one rule which should govern promotions and increases in salaries in all departments, it is because of all these things that I have said that the minister is violating the spirit of the Act, and that I have been endeavouring to criticise him in what I trust has not been in an offensive manner, but simply a manner that might be calculated to draw his attention to the undesirability of discriminating in this way and to stop such a course being followed in the future.

Mr. LEMIEUXi: I wish to add a few words to what has already been said by my friend (Mr. Pugsley). I need not say that I am a friend of the civil servants. I have always shown my sympathy with the * Civil Service in a practical way, because I know many of the civil servants; and while I do not begrudge the increases which have been given in the cases mentioned by the Minister of Finance, and whilst I also bear tribute to the officials whose salaries have been increased, I can not, however, help thinking that something should be done for another class of civil servants. On different occasions, since the beginning of this Parliament in 1911, the question of increasing the salaries of the lower officials has been mooted in this House. The House will remember that in 1913 the question came up before us and that a Bill was to be introduced by which the messengers, letter carriers and third class officials of the Civil Service were to have their salaries increased. I understand that with the war breaking out and with the heavy expenditure entailed thereby, the Government hiave found it difficult, if not impossible, to implement the promise that was made then; but with the buoyant Tevenue and with the liberalities, the largesses, that have been made in favour of some, indeed of many of the higher officials, it seems to one that the Government should, not later than this session, increase the pittance which the messengers, charwomen, letter carriers and generally speaking, the third class officials in the various departments- of the Government receive. I need not say that in the present high cost of living, it is simply impossible for the messengers, letter carriers and others to live. Not a day elapses that I do not receive letters and petitions disclosing a state of things which should not be continued if the Government can prevent it. With the present price of the necessities of life, the price of food, the price of eMhdmg, it seems to me that the 
Government should not -hesitate, and that at this session a Bill should be introduced to give to those poor Civil Servants the increases to which they are entitled. I hope that before the committee adjourns we sh-ail have a declaration on the part of the Government of their policy on this subject.
I quite agree with my -horn. friend the Minister of Finance thlat Mr. Brittain is doing excellent work in connection with the Patriotic Fund. I happen to be a member of the Pa-trdotio Fund Committee, and I can assure this committee that no man has given more unreservedly and more liberally o-f his time than has Mr. Brittain. While speaking of the Patriotic Fund-and I am here expressing only my own opinion, and I commit no one to that opinion although I have heard it expressed by many outside of this House-as this war may last for many months mpre, although we all hope it will not last so long, and as the demand upon the public will 'become more and more pressing, I think that instead of leaving the Patriotic Fund to the generosity of the public at large, the Government should impose a small tax on every Canadian in order to assist the families of our soldiers who are serving overseas. That opinion has already been expressed in the press, and even by some of the most influential members of the Patriotic Fund committee. At present some people are called on over and over again to give subscriptions to the Patriotic Fund, while hundreds of thousands who are well able to subscribe contribute nothing. The special tax need not he very heavy. A mill on the dollar might bring magnificent results. I know that some villages and towns and cities and counties have contributed very generously. I remember last winter I was asked to inaugur-afe a campaign for the Patriotic Fund in the county of Renfrew, represented by my hon. friend to my right (Mr. Graham), and I am proud to say that the town of Renfrew alone contributed $50,000 inside of a week, although on two previous occasions it had given a like amount. The county of Renfrew also subscribed $100,000, outside altogether of the town's contribution. That was a splendid example for the other counties, but I still hold the view that though there is in some cities and towns and villages and communities that broad patriotism which impels the people to do their duty towards the Patriotic Fund, the Government should make a point of seeing that the thousands and thousands who now

escape are called upon to contribute, byimposing a small tax on every Canadian from one end of the Dominion to the other. Perhaps some members of the committee share my views on this question, and will speak this evening.

I have a great deal of sympathy with what the previous speaker has said about increasing the pay of the lower grades of the Civil Service, especially as regards making it operative in the case o' the outside service as well as the inside service. I believe that none are more worthy of recognition than the letter carriers and the carriers on the rural mail routes throughout the country, and now that the Minister of Finance has somewhat loosened the bag in connection with his own department I hope that his generosity will extend to the other departments, with a view particularly to increasing the salaries of the lower grade officials.
One thing that interested me most of all in the remarks of the Minister of Finance was his statement with regard to the handling of the gold reserves of this country by the national treasury. The work has been done so well that I think the taking care of the gold reserves of this country should be left to the national treasury and its branches, and that hereafter the whole gold reserve of this country in connection with the operations of the Government and of our banks should be held in the national treasury at Ottawa. It is the beginning of a newer and a higher system of banking. It has already been adopted in the United States, where the banks now see the benefits of the gold reserves being in the custody of the Government. I think these gold reserves can be handled better and more cheaply in the national treasury than anywhere else. I think the gold reserves of this country, whether of our financial institutions or of the banks-there is a gold reserve in connection with the banks, though I cannot quite say where that gold reserve is-should be held in the national treasury and handled by the Finance Department. In speaking on this question before in the House, I have taken the ground that the nation should be at the head of the currency and banking institutions of our country, and I think the Finance Minister has given us a splendid illustration to-night of how well the nation can take hold and handle that part of our administration. When the minister comes to a revision of the banking and currency laws of this country I hope he will see his way to follow more closely the excellent
example of the United States of making the national treasury the repository of all the gold in the country.

It has nothing to do with this item, probably, but there is a matter respecting the administration of justice in Ontario on which, I think, the Dominion and Provincial Governments should get together.
The number of cases to be tried, as well as the voters' lists to be looked after in many of the counties of Ontario, does not give sufficient work for one judge. Still we find that when a vacancy occurs a second judge is appointed. In a time like this, particularly when we are trying to save every dollar that we can, when the Finance Minister is warning us to eat less, to have our clothes pressed more frequently and to buy as few new ones as we can, and all that kind of thing, the public in these counties think it is a somewhat peculiar attitude for governments to take in appointing a second judge when there is not enough work to

keep one judge warm. Take the county of Renfrew, for instance; a vacancy occurred there, and that vacancy remained for many months-I imagine it ran into years- unfilled. The one judge was not overworked; he was not kept busy; he could have doubled his work and then not have broken any union labour rules. But we found the other day a second judge appointed. The difficulty these two men now have is to divide the work which was insufficient for one man into two parts nearly equal so that each of them can have something to do. Now, what the Minister of Justice will say in regard to that I think 1 know; he will say that the Provincial Government creates the office and we fill it. The Provincial Government has the power to say whether there shall be one judge or two judges in a district or county. For a good many years there have been two judges in Renfrew, and so long as the judges were there, of course, no person would suggest that either of them should be removed. The senior judge proved to be qhite elderly, and in order to have the work performed it was necessary to appoint a junior judge to really do the work. But the senior judge having passed away, the work was continued as before by the junior judge until recently, when a senior judge was appointed. I know the Minister of Justice could decline to appoint a judge even although there was a vacancy, but I can quite see difficulties in the way of his taking that attitude when the jurisdiction of the province calls for another judge. Is there not some way by which the Minister of Justice can call the attention of the attorneys general of the various provinces to the fact that in many of the counties there is not sufficient work for one judge, and that matters might remain in statu quo where two judges are acting, but that when a vacancy occurs they ought to take into consideration the duties to be performed and ascertain if it would not be possible to have a judgeship left vacant or abolished altogether. In ordinary times it is of sufficient importance to call attention to it, but in a time like this, when every man, woman and child is expected to do his or her duty and to aid financially and in every other way in the carrying on of the war, I think the governments ought to consult together, and that where it is possible to convince the province that a judgeship need not be filled, that judgeship may at least be left vacant if not abolished altogether.

speakerposition: subtopic
Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No doubt there is a great deal in what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham says. I took the matter up a couple of years ago with the then Attorney General of Ontario looking not to a system under which the position should remain in existence and not be filled by the Government but looking to a system whereby there might be a great reduction in the number of judges and, of course, making a reduction in such places as the hon. member referred to where possibly there would not be enough work for the number of judges provided for. I certainly would be glad if the different provincial authorities would look into the matter and, where circumstances justified it, I would be very pleased if they would take such steps as might reduce the number. In the meantime it is not very easy for me to undertake to discriminate and determine whether the number of judges provided for would be justified and proceed to do the things which under the law they ought to do. I might be mistaken- about it and if I were I would be in -the unfortunate position of overriding the opinion of those who by law aTe charged with the determination of the question. But I will be very glad to act upon the suggestion again and request the provincial authorities to look into the question of the number of judges and the amount of work they are called upon to do.

I would like to endorse what my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Graham) has said and I would urge upon the minister to take the matter up as he has suggested. What'the hon. member for Renfrew said is true that in some of the counties where they have two judges they

I observed a newspaper report the . other day that the Dominion Government had advised the Imperial Government that it would be unwise for them to pass an Act concerning certain legislation passed by the Legislature of British -Columbia. My recollection of the circumstances is that the province

passed legislation and the point was raised that, owing to the expiration of the term of the legislature, for some reason, the legislation was beyond the power of -the province. An application was made to the Imperial authorities for confirmatory or declaratory legislation. The suggestion was made that the Imperial Government asked the Dominion Government for advice, and that the advice was given that it would be unwise to confirm the legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What happened was
this:	Certain legislation was enacted by
the legislature of the province of British Columbia and it was sanctioned, I think, on the 15th of March. The question that arose was whether the term of the legislature expired on the 14th of March or the 15th of March. What happened was that the legislation went through the Chamber on March 14 and was sanctioned by the Lieutenant Governor of the province only upon March 15, and there was some question in the mind of the legislators as to the validity of that legislation. The province of British Columbia considered that the proper way to remedy it was to get the Parliament of the United Kingdom to ratify that legislation. They sent forward their petition for this legislation through the Secretary of State, who forwarded it to the Imperial authorities. The latter, whether in their own mind there arose any question on the subject or not, for some reason asked this Government its opinion as to the necessity for or desirability of this legislation, and this request, by some accident, did not reach the department as promptly as it might. Tlie Imperial authorities repeated their inquiry and expressed great anxiety for an opinion. In compliance with their request, we did express an opinion on the matter on which we were asked to express an opinion, and substantially the opinion was that, whatever might have been the situation with regard to the existence of the legislature at the time of the sanctioning of this legislation, there was subsequently elected a legislature about whose power there arose no question whatsoever. This legislation, which had been enacted in that way, and which it was suggested had been sanctioned after the legislature had expired, was on a subject matter within the legislative competency of the Legislature of British Columbia, and assuming that the first legislature had expired and therefore those laws were not valid, the matter being one susceptible of being dealt with by the legisfMr. Macdonald.]
lature of the province of British Columbia, it seemed to us perfectly clear that that new Legislature of British Columbia was perfectly competent itself to ratify and validate the legislation of the previous legislature. I am just giving a statement of the substantial question. More than one piece of legislation was affected by this doubt, because, if my memory serves me, the legislation concerning which the question arose was legislation extending the term of the legislature, and, of course, if that legislation extending the term of the legislature was not valid it would affect the validity of such legislation as was enacted during tne extended term, and they desired to have all of that legislation ratified. But it seemed to us, with all respect to the advisers of the Legislature of British Columbia, to be quite clear that it was quite within the power of the new Legislature of British Columbia, concerning whose legal existence and competency there was no question, to validate that legislation and to give it retroactive effect. I do not know what action was taken by the authorities on the other side; I am inclined to believe that the Imperial authorities concurred in the advice offered to them. Upon that I do not speak positively.
I should think that all that this Government would have done would have been simply to transmit the request of the British Columbia Government to the Imperial authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is all we did.

I understand that this Government did not suggest, in the first instance, anything to the Imperial Government, but that the Imperial Government asked for advice. In that I would be inclined to think the British Government erred. I should think that if they were -going to deal with the subject at all they ought not to have asked foT advice from the Dominion Government-, because the Lieutenant Governor of a province represents the Crown.
That has been held by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and I would think that the British Columbia Government would be entitled to have the Imperial Government take such action as might be deemed proper, independently of the Dominion Government. Perhaps it would have been better if this Government had simply transmitted the request to . the Imperial Government, to be dealt with entirely by them. However, I may be wrong in that. Perhaps this Government was right in giving advice, but I would have thought

differently, having regard to the fact that the legislature of each province occupies a sovereign position as to all matters within its jurisdiction, the Lieutenant Governor representing the Sovereign in provincial matters just as the Governor General of Canada represents the Sovereign in respect of matters pertaining to the whole dominion. As this matter, therefore, was entirely out of the jurisdiction of this Government, oeing a question as between the Imperial authorities and the Government of British Columbia, I would have supposed that this Government would have simply transmitted the request to the Imperial authorities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When we transmitted the request and it went forward, they rather assumed on the other side that we were asking that the request be granted, though the intention certainly was only to transmit the request. The question addressed to us by the Imperial authorities was why this Government thought that that legislation ought to be enacted. I shall not discuss the propriety of the action of the Imperial authorities in asking us that, or the question whether they should more properly have directed such an inquiry to the Provincial Legislature. They did ask us, and it seemed to us that it was only courteous that we should answer the question. But I am not quite prepared to accept the view of the hon. gentleman that the matter was no concern of the Dominion of Canada. The British North America Act concerns the Dominion of Canada very closely, and it is not desirable that the British North America Act, at the request of a province or anybody else, should be amended, or, if I may use the expression, tinkered with, unless absolutely necessary. The British North America Act is, in a sense, our common charter; it is the charter of the dominion and of all the provinces, and I think that it is not an improper view that the Government of the Dominion is interested in any amendment of the British North America Act. It wpuld be unwise to create precedents for intervention by the home Parliament in the legislative action of provinces of this Dominion unless the circumstances rendered it absolutely necessary. One very important trust that the Dominion Government is entrusted with is the constitution of the country and, more particularly, the right to internal self-government within the Dominion, whether by provincial legislature or by the Parliament of Canada, under the British
North America Act. It behooves the Dominion Government to see that precedents for interference by the home Parliament with matters within the Dominion of Canada that fall clearly within the scope of legislative power, either of this Parliament or of the legislatures, should not be encouraged. Of course, noibody disputes the legal power of the Parliament of the United Kingdom to legislate upon any matter of this kind, even though the power has been given to Canada or to the provinces. I refer to the legal power; but the constitutional right to do it is quite another thing. It is wise to have a careful eye that you do not allow precedents for such intervention to be created, and it did seem to us in this particular matter that it would be an unfortunate precedent to establish. The request by the legislature of British Columbia implied that that legislature had not the power which it seemed to us it clearly had. Acquiescence in the request by this Government through its law officers' approval of it and approval of it hy the law officers of the home Government and by the Imperial Parliament would stand as creating a strpng presumption that the legislature of British Columbia had not the power which we believed it had 'to deal with the matter. This precedent might be invoked against any other legislature within the Dominion as constituting authoritative recognition of the proposition that the different 'legislatures had not this power. It is a duty incumbent upon those who are responsible for the control of the affairs of this Dominion to protect the right to deal within Canada with the whole field of legislation so far as regards our internal affairs. I cannot quite agree, therefore, with the suggestion that it is 'a matter of indifference to us whether the provinces acquire the habit of going straight to the Imperial Parliament and asking them to legislate for the provinces in matters clearly belonging to the legislatures themselves. I do not know that any law imposes that duty upon us, but I do not think that it is a matter of reproach to us that we should feel, as I think all Governments have felt, that it is the duty of the Canadian Government to act as a jealous custodian of the right of self-government within the limits oi this Dominion to the extent that that right is conferred upon us by the British North America Act.

I did not intend to reproach the Government at all; I simply

suggested that- the particular question which came up in this case concerned only the legislature and people of British Columbia. I did not assume for a moment that the Imperial Parliament had been asked to validate any assumed legislation except in so far as the legislature had the power to legislate, provided it was an existing body. I was taking it for granted that the legislature of British Columbia did not ask anything more than that, so that the question of legislation being ultra vires, or anything of that kind, would not be raised. I understand that the province of British Columbia thought that as the term of the legislature had expired, there was really no legislation at all, or that the whole matter was assumption. I quite agree with the Minister of Justice that the utmost care should be exercised to prevent any alteration in the British North America Act. As the British North America Act is the constitution under which the different provinces have come together, it should be jealously guarded, both by this Parliament and by the legislatures of the different provinces. I wish to explain to the minister that that was all I meant, not that the Imperial Parliament should confirm any legislation that might otherwise be ultra vires, but simply that it should confirm what the legislature professed to do and could have done if it had been a properly constituted legislature when it enacted the legislation.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The point was that we considered that that very confirmatory legislation was legislation within the power of the legislature itself.

There is this further point to be considered with regard to the matter. I quite agree with the minister that if the proposition was to amend the British North America Act with regard to any question that might trench upon the problem of jurisdiction of either the federal parliament or any of the provincial legislatures, the matter should be called to the attention of the Federal Government, but in this particular case it must be remembered that my hon. friend has, to a very great degree, created a precedent in regard to the matter. The proposition that was submitted to him was an amendment to the British North America Act, it is true, hut it was not an amendment in regard to any matter which would conflict with the jurisdiction of the Federal Parliament, and I submit with all deference, that it would have been better, and would have probably avoided a question which might arise in
[Mr. Pugsley.J
the future and from which rights could be inferred and claims could be asserted as to the Federal Parliament expressing opinions with reference to provincial legislation, if the minister had refrained from expressing an opinion upon a question which in no manner whatever interfered with or had to do with the jurisdiction of this Federal Parliament. If the question to be dealt with was one where you had legislation trenching upon federal jurisdiction, the minister would be quite within his power to state the views of his Government, but in this purely internal matter, I question whether the minister has not made a precedent which will be invoked at some future time and which will probably result in a very complicated situation. I think the minister will agree with me in that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I must say that I am glad I made the precedent, and the more the hon. member will show me that that precedent is likely to be followed, the more glad I shall be that I made it. I cannot agree with the view that it is a matter of indifference to Canada whether or not we allow a practice to grow up of abdication by the legislatures of the powers conferred upon them by the British North America Act. I thinik that if the legis-
10 p.m. lation had been passed by the Imperial Parliament, there you would have created a very unfortunate precedent, and when some other legislature, in the exercise of a power which the law advisers of this Government, would be perfectly clear belonged to it, would seek to ratify some previous legislation of its own, it would be exposed to the suggestion: But you have not such powers; and not only the legislature of British Columbia did not think it had power, since it asked for ratification at the hands of the British Parliament, but the law officers of the Dominion evidently did not think it had, because they passed that request on without observation, and when asked for an opinion, they declined to give any, but more than that, the United Kingdom Parliament considered that the legislature had not power to legislate on such a matter, since it legislated upon it itself, apparently considering such action necessary. All of the provinces are interested, and all of the provinces being interested, I think it is a matter of general interest to Canada in there not being created precedents that are of a nature to throw serious and grave doubt upon powers which they are entitled, as we believe they

are, to exercise, and I think it is very much safer to leave to the courts the determination of whether a legislature has exceeded its powers than for that legislature to be in a hurry to admit that it has, and to run to the Imperial Parliament to ask for intervention. If we were mistaken in our view, of course that would be unfortunate, just as it is unfortunate when any legal adviser gives mistaken advice; but in this particular matter, I have no reason to doubt that the view expressed was correct, and that view being correct-and I thoroughly believe it to be correct-I think there was great public interest in Canada to prevent the making of the precedent that would have been made had the legislation been enacted by the Imperial Parliament.

I wish to ask the
minister a question in regard to a matter relating to the province of Manitoba, the correspondence in connection with which has been asked for, but has not yet been brought down. I refer to the Jury Act, which was passed by the province of Manitoba, and in regard to which my hon. friend raised some exception to the right of the province to pass such legislation. I had an opportunity of looking into the matter in some slight degree, and I was somewhat surprised to find that the ground was taken by my hon. friend that legislation on the statute books of the older provinces of Canada governed' trials by juries which should be drawn and empanelled in those provinces by virtue of provincial statutes in terms practically the same a6 that to which my hon. friend took exception. I would like to know from him as to whether that statute was disallowed or what is the position of the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The correspondence was brought down and laid upon the Table of the House some time ago. The Act was not disallowed. I might further say that it is my intention, as will appear in the correspondence, to propose an amendment to the Criminal Code that will meet the difficulty, and what seems to me still to be the possible abuse that might arise by the combination of the provision of that statute of Manitoba with a provision existing in the Criminal Code. Without the correspondence before me, of course, I do not pretend to speak with absolute exactitude; but the suggestion that was made to the Manitoba Government did not proceed at all upon the ground that there was not legislative power
to enact this statute. What was pointed out was that, in view of a provision standing in the Criminal Code enabling the Crown to exercise indefinitely, to the extent of the entire panel, the right simply to "stand aside" the jurors as they were called, the legislation that made it possible to summon a very large number of jurors operative in combination with the provisions of the Criminal Code, placed the Crown in a position where it might exercise this right of "stand aside" to the extent of a very large number indeed. That seemed to us an undesirable condition to be in. I do not dispute at all that there has been legislation by other provinces which has created a similar situation, but I am quite free to admit that it had never been called to my attention. It was not legislation enacted since I have held the position which I now occupy, and I may say that I have spent my life in a province where there always was and still is a limitation upon the number of the panel to be summoned. I am perfectly free to admit that this indefinite number was quite new to me. The suggestion that was made to the Manitoba Government was merely that they should not exercise this new power until, this Parliament having met, there should be an opportunity to consider the situation created by the -removal of the limitation on the number-a situation which had existed' for some time with regard to the other provinces, but to which our attention had not been called. Perhaps there will be a better opportunity for discussion of this question when we come to discuss the Bill which is now on the Order Paper for amending the provisions of the Criminal Code, so as to put under the supervision of the judge the extent to which the absolute right to stand aside shall be exercised by the Crown. When that legislation comes down I shall have all the papers with me, and there will be every opportunity to discuss the matter, which certainly presents an interesting question with regard to criminal procedure, and as to what is understood by the constitution of the courts in the British North America Act.

What is the attitude of the Government in regard to the discharge from the penitentiaries of prisoners who desire to enlist? I understood the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) went west for the purpose of making some inquiry in reference to that. Has there been any policy adopted?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The Solicitor General, when he went on his tour of the west did, I think, look into the question of what men there were available for military service. At different times there have been suggestions, although they have never materialized, that it might be desirable to organize a regiment or battalion from among the inmates of the penitentiaries. We have not adopted a general system of granting people tickets of leave conditional upon their enlisting nor have we said we never would do it but our experience has led us to be very sparing in the issue of tickets

of leave of that kind. Proceeding with the voluntary system we found that a very strenuous objection came from the parents and' relatives of boys going into regiments against the idea of their being put in as associates of men liberated from the penitentiaries and prisons.
One can readily understand an objection on the part of parents where it is forced on their notice that their boys are to be asked to associate with criminals. But more than that, and perhaps this is a more serious objection, there is a large number of these criminals whom no one would think it desirable to put into, the ranks. There are certain classes of crimes of such a nature that it is quite undesirable to think of putting the men guilty of them into a regiment where they might corrupt their fellows. Then we have had some experience of releasing men on condition of enlistment, and in these few cases we have found quite a number of desertions. So that we have been very very sparing in the issuing of releases for enlistment. I may say that, where there existed other grounds making for the exercise of clemency, we have treated as one factor in determining a case a man's willingness to go into the service, not imposing any obligation on him. Where we thought the circumstances, taken altogether, justified release and where men have been released on ticket of leave pure and simple and have subsequently joined the forces, we have had very good reports on them, reports which have justified us in making their releases absolutely unconditional.
